summary:
Kenya criminalises consensual sex between men under the colonial-era Penal Code, with imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision applies regardless of the nationality of those involved. No statute governs gender identity and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition, although intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025. LGBTI civil-society groups may register and operate, but only within a restrictive civic space.

Document access is obstructed in practice. Evidence before the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered on 20 May 2026 by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans have been refused by civil registration offices, some having spent close to four years' wages on document corrections that never succeeded. The court found that Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.

The Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections. The petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered "gender determination" during incarceration.

Police conduct is the most immediate risk in public space. Twenty-six trans and intersex interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described routine detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, followed by on-the-spot extortion, including demands to "look for 5,000 shillings". Several of those interviewed use traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public space safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Violence is documented rather than isolated. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Kenya Human Rights Commission report "Lives on the Line" (September 2025) is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities, covering October 2023 to September 2024, and it explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

Protection machinery runs alongside that risk. The Court of Appeal ruled in 2018 that forced anal testing is unconstitutional, with compensation awarded in 2024; the Supreme Court upheld in 2023 the freedom of association that allows LGBTQ organisation registration; and a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed. "Lives on the Line" was built with more than 14 community organisations.
tangentialFactors:
Kenya's record has been shaped by litigation rather than legislation. OutRight International's profile, updated 12 March 2026, characterises the past decade as court-driven progress: the 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal finding on forced anal testing, the 2023 Supreme Court judgment on association, and the pending incitement petition.

Official hostility has been recorded at local level as well as in the courts. The US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded that in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute, while noting that the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya was permitted to register and operate. The same report found societal discrimination based on sexual orientation to be widespread, causing loss of employment and education.

Constitutional Article 28 guarantees dignity, and The Star's reporting of 23 September 2025 quotes the KHRC finding that, despite that guarantee, the data "paints a blunt picture" of violence; active LGBTIQ+ organisations nonetheless raise awareness and provide community spaces. LGBTI groups operating in a restrictive civic space is the standing position of the UK Home Office note of February 2025.

blindOutOfScope:
The national human-rights organisation's report is explicit about method: purposive sampling through organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision. Its findings are not a representative measure of prevalence, and the geography of the documented cases is not stated in the material reviewed.

Whether the state has enacted the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the High Court on 12 August 2025 is unresolved in the sources available here, as is the outcome of the pending petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The treatment of foreign nationals under the criminal provision is not specified in the sourced material; the assertion that it applies regardless of nationality comes from the earlier profile rather than from an enforcement case in the inventory.

The 2019 ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 dismissed violence claims for purported lack of evidence, and the national human-rights organisation's report challenges that finding. Whether any court has since revisited it is unresolved. The foreign government's material available dates from the 2010 reporting year and describes conditions more than a decade old.
